cutting.intro: Trim lightly to keep growth tidy and healthy.
bullets: Every 2–4 weeks in active growth, remove dead or damaged leaves and stems.
Shorten leggy shoots just above a leaf pair to improve shape and airflow.
Use clean, sharp pruners wiped before cutting to limit disease spread.

support.intro: Hydrangea macrophylla rarely needs support, but floppy stems benefit from regular checks.
bullets: Every 2–4 weeks, check tie tightness and loosen any that press into stems.
Make sure stakes stay firm after wind or rain, and guide new growth before stems lean.

aeration.intro: Light aeration helps if the soil surface starts to crust or drain slowly.
bullets: Every 1–2 months, gently loosen the top 2–3 cm (1 in) with a stick or hand fork.
Do not dig deeply, since bigleaf hydrangea has shallow roots that damage easily.

cleaning.intro: Clean-up is a light recurring task for Hydrangea macrophylla, mainly to keep foliage clear and the area tidy.
bullets: Every 2–4 weeks, wipe dusty leaves gently with a soft damp cloth or rinse lightly with water.
Remove fallen leaves and clean the pot or saucer so debris and standing water do not collect.
This improves light absorption, reduces hiding spots for pests, and keeps the plant looking neat.

humidity.intro: Extra humidity is rarely needed in moderate outdoor conditions.
bullets: Check weekly during hot, dry spells. Crisp leaf edges can suggest air that is too dry.

mulching.intro: Refresh mulch to keep root moisture and temperature more even.
bullets: Use a 5–8 cm (2–3 in) layer of compost, leaf mold, or fine bark, kept off the stems.
Top up every 2–3 months in the growing season, or sooner if the layer thins.

watering.intro: Water Bigleaf Hydrangea when the top 2–3 cm (1 in) feels dry or leaves begin to droop slightly.
bullets: Plan on watering about every 4 days, adjusting sooner in hot, dry weather and later after rain.
Soak the root zone deeply, then let excess water drain fully. Do not leave roots standing in water.
Avoid frequent shallow splashes, which wet the surface but leave deeper roots too dry.

fertilize.intro: Feed Bigleaf Hydrangea regularly during active growth.
bullets: Apply an acid-loving plant fertilizer every 2–4 weeks in spring to mid-summer, then pause by late summer.
Use at half strength on moist soil and water in well around the root zone.
Avoid overfeeding, which can cause weak growth, leaf scorch, or fewer flowers.

repotting.intro: Check regularly and repot only when needed.
bullets: Inspect every 6–12 months for roots at drainage holes, slowed growth, or water running straight through.
Move up 1 pot size, about 5–8 cm (2–3 in) wider, using compost-enriched, well-draining soil.
Repot in early spring if possible, and keep soil evenly moist after moving.

inspection.intro: Do a closer hands-on inspection every 2 weeks during active growth.
bullets: Lift and turn leaves to inspect undersides, check the stem base, and look for blockage or roots at drainage holes.
If roots are crowded, stems are soft at the base, or pests are present, follow up with repotting, pruning, or treatment.

monitoring.intro: Give Hydrangea macrophylla a quick visual review each week between other care tasks.
bullets: Look for leaf color and texture changes, steady new growth, and soil that stays slightly moist, not soggy.
Scan stems and leaf surfaces for pest activity. If anything looks off, adjust care and inspect more closely.

careDetails.aboutPlant:
Hydrangea macrophylla, commonly called bigleaf hydrangea, is a deciduous flowering shrub grown for its large summer flower heads and broad green leaves. It usually forms a rounded, leafy plant and is often seen as a mophead or lacecap type.

This species is native to Japan and is widely grown in gardens in many temperate regions. It is fairly easy to grow when moisture is steady, but heat, harsh afternoon sun, and dry soil can make care for Bigleaf Hydrangea more difficult.

It generally grows best in partial sun with consistently moist, compost-enriched, slightly acidic soil.

careAdvice.title: Protect Flower Buds
careAdvice.description: Many cultivars set next season's flower buds on old wood, so cover the shrub with frost cloth during late spring cold snaps to prevent bud loss.

careAdvice.title: Use Mulch Ring
careAdvice.description: Maintain a 5–8 cm (2–3 in) layer of bark mulch over the root zone, keeping it 5 cm (2 in) away from the stems, to reduce soil temperature swings and limit moisture stress.

careAdvice.title: Deadhead Correctly
careAdvice.description: Remove spent flower heads by cutting just above the first strong pair of buds below the bloom, which keeps the plant tidy without removing next year's flowering shoots.

careAdvice.title: Check For Mites
careAdvice.description: In hot, dry weather inspect leaf undersides for spider mites and stippling, then rinse foliage early in the day if needed, since caring for bigleaf hydrangea is easier when infestations are caught early.

soil.intro: Hydrangea macrophylla needs moisture-retentive, airy soil.
bullets: Use loamy, organic-rich soil with compost to hold moisture without compacting.
Keep drainage free with bark fines, perlite, or coarse sand mixed through heavy soil.
Aim for pH 5.5–6.5; acidic conditions suit nutrient uptake and support reliable growth.
Avoid dense clay, stagnant wet spots, and very alkaline soil that can limit vigor.

water.intro: Consistent soil moisture is important for steady growth and flowering.
bullets: Check soil before watering and water deeply when the top 2–5 cm (1–2 in) feels slightly dry.
Hydrangea macrophylla often needs water about every 4 days in warm weather, but less often in cool or rainy periods.
Fast wilting and crisp leaf edges suggest drought, while yellowing leaves, soggy soil, and root decline suggest poor drainage or overwatering.

soilPH.intro: Slightly acidic soil is important for healthy growth and nutrient uptake.
bullets: Hydrangea macrophylla grows best at pH 5.5–6.5 and prefers acidic rather than neutral or alkaline soil.
Test pH with a soil meter or lab kit. Lower pH with sulfur or peat moss, or raise it slightly with garden lime if needed.
Wrong pH can cause nutrient lock-out, leaf chlorosis, weak growth, and reduced flowering.

pruning.intro: Hydrangea macrophylla needs light pruning to manage shape and preserve flowering.
bullets: Prune just after flowering in summer, since buds for next year form on older stems.
Remove dead, damaged, weak, or crowded stems first to improve airflow and structure.
Cut spent flower heads back to a healthy pair of buds for a tidier form.
Use clean, sharp pruners and avoid hard pruning, which can reduce next season blooms.

humidity.intro: Bigleaf hydrangea prefers 40–60% humidity and manages average outdoor air well.
bullets: Dry air is tolerated briefly, but prolonged low humidity can crisp leaf edges and wilt soft growth.
Humidity stress shows as browning margins, drooping in heat, and faster soil drying.
Raise humidity with mulch, grouped planting, and steady soil moisture rather than misting.

sunlight.intro: Hydrangea macrophylla grows best with balanced outdoor light.
bullets: Provide 4–6 hours of sun daily, ideally gentle morning sun with afternoon shade in warm climates.
Bigleaf hydrangea tolerates partial shade and bright filtered light, but less than 3–4 hours often reduces flowering.
Strong midday or afternoon sun can scorch leaves and dry buds in summer; slightly more sun is tolerated in cooler seasons.

container.intro: This species can grow well in containers with careful moisture and root-space management.
bullets: Use a pot with several drainage holes so excess water leaves quickly after each watering.
Choose a container about 30–45 cm (12–18 in) wide and similarly deep to buffer drying and support roots.
Pick a heavier pot material if needed, because broad leafy growth and flower heads can make plants top-heavy.

placement.intro: Place this shrub outdoors in bright, sheltered conditions.
bullets: Bigleaf Hydrangea is best grown in the ground outside, not as a long-term indoor plant.
Choose morning sun with afternoon shade, such as an east-facing border, with about 90–150 cm (36–60 in) space for airflow.
Avoid harsh midday sun, exposed windy sites, and spots near heating vents, cold drafts, or reflected wall heat.

fertilizer.intro: Bigleaf hydrangea benefits from light feeding during active growth.
bullets: Use an acid-loving, balanced NPK fertilizer or slow-release formula, plus compost in spring.
Feed every 4–6 weeks in spring and summer, or apply slow-release once as directed.
Use at 1/2 strength for liquid feeds to avoid soft, weak growth.
Stop feeding in late autumn and winter while the plant is dormant.

winterCare.intro: Winter care matters because flower buds and young stems can be damaged by hard frost.
bullets: Mulch the root zone with 5–8 cm (2–3 in) of compost or bark.
Wrap exposed stems with burlap in colder areas to reduce bud loss.
Water during dry winter spells if soil is not frozen.
Move container plants to a sheltered, unheated spot before severe freezes.

propagation.intro: Hydrangea macrophylla is commonly propagated from cuttings, and seeds are slower.
bullets: Take softwood cuttings in late spring to early summer from non-flowering shoots.
Root cuttings in moist, free-draining mix with high humidity and bright, indirect light.
Sow seeds on the surface in spring and keep them evenly moist and warm.
Use clean tools and remove lower leaves to limit rot and improve rooting success.

temperature.intro: Steady, mild temperatures support the best growth and flowering.
bullets: Aim for 59–75°F (15–24°C) during active growth, with fewer stress symptoms in cool nights and mild days.
Established plants tolerate winter cold to about 5°F (-15°C), but late spring frost can damage swelling buds and young shoots.
Prolonged heat above 86°F (30°C) can reduce bloom quality and increase wilting, so afternoon shade helps in hot summer weather.

repottingAndTransplanting.intro: Transplanting is more common than repotting for this outdoor shrub.
bullets: Move it in early spring or autumn, when temperatures are mild and soil stays evenly moist.
Repot only if roots circle the pot, drainage is poor, or growth slows noticeably.
Shift to a container 5–10 cm (2–4 in) wider, or replant at the same soil depth.
Water deeply after moving and disturb the root ball as little as possible to reduce stress.

facts.text: In many cultivars, flower color can vary with soil chemistry. More acidic soils often produce blue flowers, while less acidic soils tend to produce pink flowers because aluminum becomes more or less available to the plant.

facts.text: This species is native to Japan and has been cultivated there for a long time. It later became one of the most widely grown ornamental hydrangeas in gardens around the world.

facts.text: Bigleaf hydrangea includes cultivar groups with different flower-head forms. Mopheads have dense rounded clusters, while lacecaps have a flatter head with showy outer sterile flowers around smaller fertile flowers.

interestingFacts.didYouKnow: Although often linked with ornamental flowers, all parts of this species contain cyanogenic glycosides and are considered toxic to humans and animals if ingested.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Powdery mildew
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Remove badly affected leaves and thin crowded growth to improve air movement. Water at soil level, avoid wetting foliage late in the day, and use a sulfur- or potassium bicarbonate-based fungicide if the problem persists.
pestsAndDiseases.description: This disease causes a white, dusty coating on leaves, stems, and flower buds, especially in mild weather with poor airflow. Heavy infection can distort new growth and reduce flowering quality.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Cercospora leaf spot
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Pick up fallen leaves and remove heavily spotted foliage to reduce reinfection. Keep mulch in place to limit soil splash, water at the base, and apply a labeled leaf spot fungicide if outbreaks are repeated.
pestsAndDiseases.description: This disease causes small purple to brown spots on older leaves, often starting near the lower part of the plant in warm, humid weather. Severe spotting can lead to early leaf drop by late summer.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Botrytis blight
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Cut off infected flowers and dead plant material promptly and keep the shrub open with light pruning. Avoid overhead watering during cool, wet periods, and use a labeled ornamental fungicide when conditions strongly favor spread.
pestsAndDiseases.description: This disease affects flower heads and tender leaves, causing brown, water-soaked patches and gray fuzzy mold in cool, damp conditions. Blooms may rot before they dry properly on the shrub.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Aphids
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Wash colonies off with a firm stream of water and prune out heavily infested tips. Encourage natural predators and use insecticidal soap on young growth if populations keep returning.
pestsAndDiseases.description: These insects cluster on soft new shoots and buds, sucking sap and causing curled leaves, sticky honeydew, and distorted growth. They are most noticeable in spring and early summer.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Hydrangea scale
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Inspect stems closely and wipe or prune out infested sections when numbers are low. Treat crawler stages with horticultural oil during the growing season, and consider a dormant oil application in late winter where appropriate.
pestsAndDiseases.description: These insects attach to stems and leaf undersides, where they feed on sap and weaken the plant over time. Symptoms include yellowing leaves, sticky residue, and reduced vigor.

faqs.question: Warum blüht meine Bauernhortensie nicht gut?

faqs.answer: Ja, sie wächst gut in großen Behältern mit Drainage. Verwenden Sie einen Topf mit mindestens 30–45 cm (12–18 in) Durchmesser und erwarten Sie eine schnellere Austrocknung als bei Pflanzen im Boden. Dies ist wichtig, wenn Sie Bauernhortensien auf Terrassen anbauen.
